principle: Give one director the final say; never settle design by majority vote
why: In creative work, more votes don't make an answer right. Majority decisions converge on the safest, most mediocre ideas, and ideas everyone opposed in planning often turn out fun once built. A team usually has one director because the role charts the game's path, and split opinions or unclear goals derail it. That power demands a balanced view and good information, or direction turns into dictatorship.
how_to_apply: Name one person who holds the whole-game vision and makes the content calls. If you split the role (co-leads on a jam team, say), write down exactly who decides what. When the team is split, the director decides and explains the reasoning. Polls are fine as input or out of curiosity, but the decision and any later adjustments stay with the director. If the person with the vision believes in an unpopular idea, build it and judge it in the game.
anti_pattern: Counting hands on design questions; co-directors with no clear final say; a leader barking orders with paper-thin reasoning.
example: Metal Gear Solid 3's wound-treatment system reportedly had only four supporters on its team at first, yet it is fun in the finished game. Sakurai polled his team on Mii Fighter maid outfits out of curiosity; they went with A, and he then made a director's call to color the socks white because brighter extremities make movement easier to read.
review_question: For each open design question, can everyone name the one person who will decide it?
keywords: director final say decision-making majority vote democracy consensus design by committee authority one vision co-director lead designer

principle: Hold the concept steady and steer with small, frequent corrections
why: Sakurai calls the concept a lighthouse: change direction midway and the team gets lost, months of art and programming get thrown away, and morale drops. But individual decisions set the trajectory toward that light, and a wrong one should be corrected rather than defended, so frequent slight adjustments keep the project on course. Many teammates won't feel a new game's appeal from documents until it's playable, so the director has to keep them oriented.
how_to_apply: Before production, write the concept as one sentence of appeal (his examples: the fun of sending opponents flying, the thrill of sprinting down a straight path) and don't start full production until it's that clear. When fatigue or doubt sets in, check decisions against the concept instead of changing course. Correct individual calls as soon as you see they're wrong, amplify emergent fun that still heads toward the concept, and before scrapping a part, count the months of work and the morale you'd lose. Keep restating the concept to the team.
anti_pattern: Changing the game's direction because it isn't turning out as expected; clinging to a known-bad decision because it was already made; swinging the direction back and forth with each round of feedback.
example: People have told Sakurai after a project shipped, "Now I see what you were getting at", which is why he says design documents alone rarely convey the fun.
review_question: Has any recent change altered what the game's core appeal is, or only how we get there?
keywords: concept vision direction course correction pivot change direction midway lighthouse steering iteration spec change emergent fun north star

principle: Raise problems the moment you see them, with facts and a fix
why: Players can only complain; developers can still fix things. Staying quiet and saying "I knew that was wrong!" afterwards only satisfies your ego and upsets teammates. Decisions are only as good as their information: act on an incorrect premise and everything after it is wrong. The worst case is someone who struggles silently and says at the deadline that they can't do it, losing the time an early fix would have saved. Pairing each problem with a proposed solution keeps the environment constructive.
how_to_apply: Make it a team rule with no exceptions: tell someone who can act, right away, with everything you know, and don't waste time arguing about how to bring it up. Bring the problem and at least one possible fix as a set. Flag being stuck well before the deadline with an honest status, and treat that report as a baton pass. If the team decides to keep things as they are, ask for their reasons and accept them.
anti_pattern: Saving objections for after the project; struggling silently until the deadline; only saying "this isn't good"; teams arguing over how to raise a problem instead of raising it.
example: Sakurai prefers that people tell him everything they know, leaving nothing out, because the less accurate the information, the more likely the decision is a mistake.
review_question: Is anyone stuck or worried about something the decision-maker hasn't heard yet?
keywords: raise issues early speak up escalate report problems blockers stuck honest status bad news proposed solution transparency psychological safety

principle: Decide on the spot instead of putting decisions off until later
why: Each decision is a fork that sends the team down a long production path, and every minute they wait is a minute the issue stays unresolved. Wanting to be careful and get second opinions is understandable, but there often isn't time for that hesitation, and a quick, firm decision helps more of the team than you'd imagine. Delaying a key member's decision can put their whole team behind schedule.
how_to_apply: Make sure someone with the authority to decide is in each decision meeting, and push them to decide before it ends. If you're the decider, make the call as soon as a teammate brings you the issue; if information is missing, research it right away. Put every option on the table, pick the one that works in the short and long term, and leave leeway to correct it.
anti_pattern: Ending a meeting with "I'll have to decide on this later!"; long deliberation while the team is blocked.
example: Sakurai says he tries to make a call as soon as a team member comes to him, doing any research he needs on the spot.
review_question: Which decisions are open right now, and who is waiting on each one?
keywords: decision making decide quickly decisiveness indecision blocked waiting meetings postpone defer analysis paralysis fast calls

principle: Show, don't tell: give visual feedback as quick retouches and sketches
why: Changes to palette, contrast, mood or pose are hard to put into words, and text-only notes, especially remote ones, get misread. Showing communicates more clearly than telling, and a retouch that takes about five minutes, ten at most, is more efficient than a verbal explanation. Concrete visuals early in a project also help the team move forward with confidence.
how_to_apply: For any visual note, spend 5-10 minutes on a rough paintover, a mouse sketch, a photo of a posed figure or a diagram, and send it side by side with the original plus one line on what to change. Label it as an example of the direction; the artist still does the release-quality work. Save retouches for what words can't carry, because nobody can retouch everything.
anti_pattern: Long verbal descriptions of visual changes; treating the director's retouch as final art; trying to retouch every asset.
example: Sakurai retouched Smash Bros. Ultimate backgrounds (a Spirits exploration cave with a too-understated palette, the Marx boss fight, a World of Light path) in Photoshop using only a mouse, and posed a figure to show how upper-body twist adds information to Sora's forward aerial.
review_question: Does every visual note on this asset come with an image that shows the change?
keywords: paintover retouch draw over redline visual feedback art direction supervision show don't tell sketch mockup reference image posed figure

principle: Make every note concrete enough to act on without guessing
why: Vague notes make people guess what's in your head, which costs them extra work and extra rounds. Specific notes let the team fix each problem. For things that can't be drawn, like sound, an email asking for more "clang" or "boom" tells people you had something in mind but not what. Words also mean different things to different people, so notes can come back as the exact opposite of what you asked for.
how_to_apply: Name the exact change: the axis, the spacing, the repetition, the frame. For sound, state the role ("this is a strong attack"), compare only to sounds everyone knows ("like a jet engine") and attach a link to a real example. With a reference track, say which quality to keep and which signature element not to copy. When revisions keep contradicting your notes, play the reference together and check you mean the same thing by the key terms. If you lack a craft's vocabulary, route notes through someone who has it. Send notes as bullet points.
anti_pattern: "Make it look better"; onomatopoeia-only sound notes; assuming everyone knows the sound or song you have in mind; repeating the same note louder.
example: Arrangements of the Athena theme kept coming back opposite to Sakurai's feedback because he and the musicians meant different melodies by "main melody". On the Mishima Dojo wall he asked for the X-axis to stay flat with jagged edges only on Y and Z.
review_question: Could the recipient act on each note without asking what you meant?
keywords: specific feedback actionable notes vague critique sound feedback audio references onomatopoeia shared vocabulary terminology misunderstanding bullet points

principle: Give feedback to everyone involved at once, in the open
why: Relaying intent down a chain (director to planner to programmers) can return the polar opposite of what was meant. When every discipline hears the same explanation, everyone understands the goals, anyone unsure knows what to do whatever their role, and visibility improves on large projects. Seeing the feedback others get, not just your own, lets the whole team learn and avoid the same missteps.
how_to_apply: When reviewing a feature, gather everyone who touches it (planner, programmers, modelers, animators, effects, sound, and their leads), show the build on a big screen, use a mic if the room needs it, take questions at the end, and let anyone sit in. Hold group reviews within each discipline. When a review needs changes, explain them to everyone involved, not only the person who asked. Keep these sessions speedy, or the extra meeting time stops paying off.
anti_pattern: Briefing only the planner and hoping it trickles down; private critique the rest of the team never hears; group meetings that drag on.
example: After instructions relayed through planners on Kid Icarus: Uprising came back reversed, Sakurai required every relevant member to attend his feedback from Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U onward: about 30 people on average, up to 50, in a room with a huge monitor.
review_question: Did everyone who will touch this feature hear the feedback first-hand?
keywords: group review feedback session all-hands telephone game relay miscommunication visibility shared critique dailies review meeting

principle: Answer every review request the same day it arrives
why: The longer a reply takes, the longer teammates wait, and delaying a key member's decision can put their whole team behind. Quick replies make the second and third review rounds easier, while putting them off makes the next day more miserable. Late-night reviews also wreck the reviewer's sleep.
how_to_apply: Use one predictable channel (his is an email titled "Review Request", sent once the production work is finished), handle requests first come, first served, and reply the same day, ideally right after the review you're on. Set a delivery cutoff so reviews don't start late at night (his was 8 PM). Block a fixed daily period, such as mornings, with no reviews so your own work gets done.
anti_pattern: Unread review requests piling up overnight; being open to reviews all day so your schedule breaks into pieces; starting reviews at 11 PM.
example: Sakurai replies to every review email within the day no matter how many pile up. For this channel, HIKE had to deliver by 8 PM, and each episode got about six to eight rounds of bullet-point feedback.
review_question: Is any review request or approval older than one working day?
keywords: review turnaround approvals same day response latency bottleneck supervision inbox cutoff time focus time feedback loop

principle: Write specs teammates can build from without guessing
why: Spec sheets carry the detail that programmers, animators and other staff build from, and anything vague gets misread or never made. As Sakurai puts it, it's not just you who needs to understand your game. Exact numbers, units and visuals let values land close the first time and let you spot errors when the build doesn't match the spec.
how_to_apply: For animation, give an animation list with each move's length and when the attack becomes active, posed-figure photos for key poses, and four values per attack: standby pose, attack pose, attack start frame, and total frames until it can be canceled. Write timing in frames, not "quick", and give every speed a unit. Put each tunable value in plain-language brackets ("[Special startup X-velocity is O]") so programmers know what to expose. Script every grunt before a voice session. Tell artists and animators each piece's gameplay role (which surfaces have collision, when a hit lands). Tidy your private outline before it goes on the shared server.
anti_pattern: "Fast" or "slow" instead of frame counts; speeds without units; terse parameter names others misread; a raw personal idea dump posted as the spec.
example: An average Smash fighter's spec includes 70-80 pages of posed-figure images, and Sakurai's rule is that anything inside brackets becomes a parameter.
review_question: If you handed this spec to a new teammate, what would they have to ask you?
keywords: spec sheet design document GDD requirements animation brief frame data parameters units handoff documentation clarity planner

principle: Start specs from the player's ideal, then negotiate feasibility with programmers
why: Design documents often come back prioritizing the developers' jobs, but players only care whether the game is good and won't cut you slack because development was hard. Hedging with "we could do A, or we could do B" pushes the decision onto someone else. The proposal is the game's skeleton, so don't twist it out of shape for efficiency up front: start from the ideal and course-correct for cost.
how_to_apply: Choose the one option you judge best and delete the Plan B from proposals. Flag every choice made for development convenience and keep it only if players won't suffer for it. Bring programmers in to balance the ideal against what's technically feasible, take the team's suggestions with an open mind, and fall back to an alternative only when real problems appear.
anti_pattern: Specs that put ease of development ahead of the player; proposals that list alternatives instead of making a choice.
example: Sakurai's answer to convenience-first design documents: players aren't concerned about why developers do what they do, only whether the game is good.
review_question: Which parts of this spec exist for our convenience rather than the player's experience?
keywords: player first ideal spec plan B hedging feasibility programmer collaboration compromise developer convenience proposal commit

principle: Make sure everyone knows the goal and their piece's role in it
why: Roles only produce a game when they work in tandem, and nothing gets done without mutual understanding. Art made without knowing its gameplay function can bury the terrain; animators who think gameplay is the designers' job put weak poses on the hit frame; people who match a reference without grasping a character's essence miss what makes it feel right. And everyone finishing their assigned tasks doesn't guarantee a finished game.
how_to_apply: Share the project's objectives with every role, not only the leads, and mix professions in subteams with the director involved in each. Tell artists which elements have collision, tell animators when and where collision is active, and give everyone working on a character a short statement of its core essence. Keep a visible picture of everything still needed to ship.
anti_pattern: Treating art as standalone pictures; assuming the game will ship because everyone completed their own list.
example: A Mii Fighter Nakoruru costume matched her King of Fighters XIV look but felt off until a revision captured her essence. Sakurai's common stage note: "your backdrop's outshining your terrain."
review_question: Can each teammate say what the game is about and why their current task matters to it?
keywords: shared goals alignment vision context role clarity big picture purpose understanding cross-discipline subteams essence

principle: Show the whole team the whole game, every day
why: On big projects people can be like a worker making one screw without knowing it becomes a car, and working without the larger picture is stressful. Team-wide emails often go unread, but a page with something new every day gets read on people's own initiative. For a director joining an existing team, regular reports also mean the team isn't taking direction from a total stranger.
how_to_apply: Post a daily report: one current screenshot at the top, then 3-5 topics (news, what you're working on, checklists, issues to fix, and sometimes a game you played or current events), with comments open. Put key announcements there instead of in mass email, and invite teammates to post what they finished. Every few months, or every period, have each discipline or subteam present its finished work to everyone, even though scheduling it is a hassle.
anti_pattern: Relying on mass email for important information; skipping team presentations because they're hard to organize.
example: Sakurai wrote a Daily Report every working day from Smash Bros. Brawl on. When he said he'd reveal the next fighter (Sephiroth) there at 5 p.m., the dev team alone brought the server down.
review_question: When did every team member last see the current build as a whole?
keywords: daily report standup status update newsletter screenshot of the day progress visibility information sharing showcase demo day team presentation

principle: Playtest with fresh outsiders and children, and watch instead of asking
why: Developers know the game too well to be the standard. An outsider who has played grows familiar too, so you can't call the same person back as fresh a second or third time. Children always give honest reactions, showing where controls are hard and what bores them. Problems some players have, like 3D motion sickness, stay invisible on a team where nobody feels them.
how_to_apply: With permission, invite staff members' children and their friends, make it feel like a fun session with snacks, stand back and note where they struggle or lose interest. Rotate in new testers who start from the very beginning, treating each one as a one-time first impression. Recruit testers prone to motion sickness to check camera comfort. Share the reactions with the team.
anti_pattern: Asking testers what they think instead of watching what they do; reusing an outsider as if they were still fresh; signing off on difficulty or comfort with only the team's judgment.
example: Playing the original Super Smash Bros., one child shouted "Whoa! Look how far he flew!" at a Falcon Punch's knockback.
review_question: When did someone who had never played this build play it from the start while we watched in silence?
keywords: playtesting user testing outside testers fresh eyes children kids observation first impressions usability motion sickness blind test

principle: Delegate execution to specialists and testers; keep the director supervising
why: On the early Smash games, Kirby Air Ride, Meteos and Kid Icarus: Uprising, Sakurai entered or decided every parameter himself on top of supervision, approvals and marketing, which he says he should never have done; on the earliest games it took all he had just to finish. Dedicated play testers who battle every day are more attuned to balance than the director. Specialists do their best work on pieces they're attached to or excel at, and some playful details are better left to trusted partners than dictated.
how_to_apply: Build tools and pipelines so a few planners can enter and tune data; staff dedicated play testers and trust their analysis; give specialties such as post-processing a clear owner. Let composers pick pieces they're attached to, and otherwise assign by strength. Keep the director playing the build and supervising instead of doing data entry.
anti_pattern: A director who is the only person able to change values; dictating every detail of creative work you've handed off.
example: From Smash Bros. for 3DS/Wii U a small team of planners handled tuning, and on Ultimate Sakurai only supervised. He still plays about 30 minutes of multiplayer at lunch. HIKE designed this channel's Grab Bag gesture visuals with no instruction from him.
review_question: What is the director doing personally that someone else could do as well or better?
keywords: delegation trust specialists play testers planners tuning parameters bottleneck micromanagement director workload ownership

principle: Step in personally when delegated core work stalls
why: Trusting people with their work doesn't mean leaving a stalled core alone indefinitely. When assets already exist, clear new specs and a director's return can rescue a project quickly. Sakurai remembers Iwata never telling him how to approach his games' content, yet jumping in to help teams whenever problems arose.
how_to_apply: Let leads own their work, but watch the core: if the central gameplay still isn't working after a long stretch, step back in, write fresh specs and rebuild the logic on the finished assets. When tuning stops giving the results you expect, have strong programmers hunt for code bugs, since no parameter can fix broken code. When someone reports they're stuck, take the baton and reassign, re-scope or change approach.
anti_pattern: Leaving stalled core gameplay delegated indefinitely; dictating content when what the team needs is hands-on help.
example: After a year of delegated development on Kirby Air Ride, not a single Warp Star worked right. At the lead programmer's request Sakurai returned as director, they wrote new specs, and the game was finished in three and a half months, with courses and machines mostly done. In Melee's final stretch Iwata worked directly with the programmers to find code bugs.
review_question: Is any delegated core system still not working after repeated attempts?
keywords: intervene rescue stalled project step in rebuild hands-on leadership unblock escalation director involvement trust

principle: As director, own the trimming when plans slip
why: Hardware limits, delayed deadlines and growing workloads always knock plans off course. It's faster when the director recognizes the problems and cuts than when compromises come out of battles between cost-focused producers and quality-focused directors. Just about any finished game is the result of trimming and hard work.
how_to_apply: When plans slip, anticipate the damage and offload the heavy or flammable cargo: drop or scale back the riskiest work and reset the course. Cut detail no player will see, but allow harmless extras that cost no schedule or performance. Set hard requirements early and pare content until they hold. Before the costliest late phase, check whether the project can actually be finished. Thank the team at the end, because finishing usually means painful cuts.
anti_pattern: Waiting for a producer to force the cuts; spending effort on details nobody will ever see.
example: Sakurai asked the stage team to tone down car tires that turned in the backdrop of Inkling's stage, something truly nobody would see. On Smash for 3DS he considered 60 FPS an absolute must and pared things down until it held.
review_question: What are we still building that we'd cut if we were honest about the schedule?
keywords: scope cuts trimming triage prioritization cut features schedule slip deadline overscope feature creep kill your darlings

principle: Protect individuality: intervene when tuning sands distinctiveness down
why: Balancing purely on strength levels everything out: weaknesses get patched, strengths get cut, and every character ends up average, and average is mediocre. Sakurai wants each fighter highly unique and player opinions divided, and accepts some unfairness in isolated parts for it. Echo chambers and outside pressure can push a game toward the ordinary, while a unique vision gives it distinctive strength.
how_to_apply: Delegate balance analysis, but have the director step in mainly when a proposed change threatens a character's or the game's individuality. Tell the tuning team to keep characters unique by amplifying shortcomings to offset advantages. Listen to the team's concerns and adapt to them, but separate those from pressure that would only make the game more ordinary.
anti_pattern: Sanding every outlier toward the mean; letting every loud opinion steer the design.
example: Sakurai says that when he does speak up about Smash balance, it's most often because a fighter's individuality is being threatened.
review_question: Has this round of changes made any character or system less distinctive?
keywords: individuality uniqueness distinctiveness character identity balance homogenization average mediocre vision protect quirks echo chamber

principle: Judge work by its purpose, not your mental image, and know when to stop
why: The director's goal isn't to make everything conform to personal ideals. Work that differs from what you pictured is fine if it meets the goal and the quality is there, and sometimes it turns out better. Supervision often brings a half-step when you hoped for a whole one, and swinging big and then pulling back can feel like changing direction every round; the director and the artist share responsibility for the result.
how_to_apply: State each asset's goal in one sentence (for the dojo wall: it must look like wooden boards actually broke) and approve anything that meets it. Approve sounds that fit the game even when they differ from what you imagined. Flag flaws as soon as you see them, but if several rounds still don't reach the bar, put it in the game as-is and spend your time elsewhere. Aim for first-try approvals by being clear about what you want from the start.
anti_pattern: Rejecting good work for not matching the picture in your head; feedback rounds that never end; swinging direction each round.
example: Smash Ultimate's Mishima Dojo destructible wall took several rounds of retouched feedback (sawn-looking cuts, boards twisting like metal, copy-pasted patterns, splinters hanging into the fighters' path) before it read as broken wood. Sakurai says he accepts work and moves on surprisingly often.
review_question: What is this asset's one-sentence goal, and does the current version meet it?
keywords: acceptance criteria approval good enough diminishing returns feedback rounds perfectionism convergence definition of done ship it

principle: Lead by request and respect, never by rank
why: People with ideas are powerless without others. A director's instructions travel downstream, but they are really requests made from the bottom up to the people doing the work. Nobody likes a demanding customer, so acting superior only breeds resentment. Every teammate is an ally, and a disagreement doesn't make you enemies. The industry is small, so fights and badmouthing come back to you.
how_to_apply: Phrase direction as requests to the people who'll do the work. Address everyone politely in name and tone, including brand-new and much younger hires. Treat disagreements as normal between allies. Raise issues as constructive feedback about the work, never as complaints about a person behind their back. Don't act subservient either, and leave every team on good terms.
anti_pattern: Barking orders; acting superior or subservient; badmouthing coworkers; abandoning a project midway to jump to the next job.
example: Sakurai addresses team members politely even when they're new hires much younger than him. Directors at other companies sometimes ask him about former teammates who are interviewing with them.
review_question: Would the team describe the lead's instructions as requests or as orders?
keywords: respect leadership style humility hierarchy rank politeness team culture conflict ally reputation small industry

principle: Meet trouble with calm analysis and shared responsibility, not blame
why: Sakurai remembers Iwata using logic rather than instinct: where most people would lose their temper or take offense, he stayed calm and offered analysis or suggestions. Results come from a whole chain (visuals, title, advertising, competing titles, timing, platform), so poor sales can't be pinned on one person, and in supervision the director and the artist share responsibility.
how_to_apply: When something goes wrong, analyze the cause and propose a fix before reacting. In post-release reviews, look across the whole chain instead of naming a culprit. Treat friction between roles as a question of mutual support: what can you do so the other side can do their best work?
anti_pattern: Losing your temper or taking offense; pinning a failure on a single person.
example: Sakurai credits Iwata, by then head of Nintendo's corporate planning division, with working directly alongside the programmers to find the code bugs stalling Melee.
review_question: When we last reviewed a problem, did we analyze causes or look for someone to blame?
keywords: blame calm conflict resolution blameless postmortem analysis temper shared responsibility failure review sales flop

principle: Give everyone an open, answered channel for opinions and requests
why: People with different skills, standpoints and tastes notice different problems, in the game and in how the team is run, but some won't speak up unless it's easy. Hearing everyone matters even if some posts get lost. After a big change in how a team works, many people share the same problems, and asking early surfaces them.
how_to_apply: Set up an opinion board where anyone can post about how development is going, and have the director reply with their thinking or forward items to the right team. Survey everyone soon after a big workflow change and fix the common problems first. Make time for one-on-ones. On the listening end, be flexible and decide quickly.
anti_pattern: Posts that get lost with no reply; assuming people will raise things without an easy way to do it.
example: Sakurai set up an opinions board whenever he joined a team. His survey shortly after Smash Ultimate went remote in April 2020 found shared problems with desks and chairs, reference monitors, internet, playtesting and social contact.
review_question: Where can the most junior teammate post a concern today, and who answers it?
keywords: opinion board suggestion box feedback channel survey one-on-one listening team voice input retrospective

principle: Separate the director's content role from the producer's business role
why: The director has the final call on content and is best placed to own the concept, since shaping it is hard without a grasp of the game's core appeal. Producers weigh development cost against projected sales, handle staffing and marketing (a good game doesn't matter if nobody knows about it) and take interviews because directors are busy and essential to the team. Their viewpoints differ, but both want a quality product.
how_to_apply: Write down who owns content and concept and who owns budget, staffing and publicity. On a tiny team one person can wear both hats, but know which hat a decision belongs to. Build enough trust that differences of opinion don't turn into standoffs. If you go independent, estimate how much company management would eat your creative time before you hire.
anti_pattern: Handing the concept to someone who doesn't grasp the core appeal; letting cost-versus-quality fights stand in for decisions.
example: Sakurai often slots into a producer's role because Smash fighter reveal movies are marketing. He runs Sora Ltd. with almost no production staff so management doesn't eat his directing time.
review_question: Who owns the concept, and who owns the budget, staffing and publicity?
keywords: director producer roles responsibilities budget staffing marketing publicity concept owner team structure business creative split

principle: Budget for overhead: ten people produce about seven people's work
why: Running a team takes management time: someone has to handle workloads, outside communication and creative supervision, and a strong creator promoted to lead stops producing their old output. The bigger the team, the longer it takes to get everyone on the same page, including tools, security and rules. Big changes cost output too: Sakurai estimated remote work cut productivity by about 30%.
how_to_apply: Plan at roughly 70% effective output from headcount, with more overhead as the team grows. Name who handles workload management, external communication and quality supervision. Backfill a promoted lead's production work. Set up shared tools and rules early. On a team of just a few people, expect closer to full output.
anti_pattern: Planning as if headcount equals output; expecting a newly promoted lead to keep their old individual output.
example: Sakurai's rule of thumb: depending on the situation, ten people can generally produce seven people's worth of work.
review_question: Does our schedule assume everyone spends all their time producing?
keywords: management overhead team size productivity estimation scheduling headcount capacity planning lead promotion remote work

principle: Give every task and bug a ticket with one owner and a status
why: Work that lives only in conversation slips through the cracks; whoever holds a ticket owns the work, so responsibility and progress are obvious. Bugs found on old builds don't help, programmers aren't always the right fixers, and every fix risks a new bug, so a disciplined loop beats carefulness alone.
how_to_apply: Split each content piece into tickets per discipline (spec, model and rig, animation, programming, effects, sound effects, balancing), each with one owner, a status and a deadline a lead reviews, and leave slack between dependent tasks. For bugs: test only on the latest daily build, file a ticket once the bug can be reproduced, grade severity (Class S for hangs and save corruption, Class A for progression blockers), route it to the discipline that owns the problem, have the tester verify the fix in several configurations, and mark it resolved instead of deleting it.
anti_pattern: Tasks with no owner; downstream staff forced to start on unfinished upstream work; sending every bug to programmers; deleting closed tickets.
example: Smash Bros. sometimes ran CPU battles all night to find bugs, and near a project's end testers in Japan, North America and Europe pass save data back and forth.
review_question: Does every open task and bug have exactly one owner and a current status?
keywords: tickets task tracking bug tracker issue ownership status severity triage QA reproduction steps regression daily build

principle: Present ideas fast: core idea first, no justifications or alternatives
why: Creators have to communicate their ideas, and Sakurai's secret is speed: trim the fat and get to the heart of the topic. Speed isn't the same as short; a 200-page proposal works if each page moves quickly like a comic panel. A wall of text read aloud is annoying because people just read ahead. Defining a new game by comparison invites the question of why not just play the original.
how_to_apply: Open with the core idea and drop justifications, alternatives and Plan B. Use one image and about two lines of text per slide, group slides into categories so people know where they are, and talk around the slides instead of reading them. Explain even the basics simply. Describe what's new rather than "X, but with Y".
anti_pattern: Long preambles; reading slides aloud; pitching a new game as a variant of an existing one.
example: Sakurai's Smash Bros. Ultimate proposal ran over 200 PowerPoint pages, nearly all one image and two lines of text, presented quickly.
review_question: Does the pitch open with the core idea, with no justifications or alternatives in the way?
keywords: presentations pitching proposals slides meetings communication brevity speed clarity deck

principle: Build a warm team: thank, celebrate and play together
why: Sakurai sees a good director-team relationship as the way game development should be. Small fun events act as icebreakers, captioning the daily screenshot helped the team unwind, and kid playtests drove the team forward through hard stretches. Finishing usually means tough decisions and cut content, so master-up can feel wounding, and that's when thanks matter most.
how_to_apply: Turn giveaways into quick games (list items on the daily page, let people sign up, pick winners by rock-paper-scissors, a match in your own game or a secret rule). Keep snacks in the review room. Thank the staff explicitly at master-up. When forming a core team, favor people who love the game or genre.
anti_pattern: Handing things out at random; treating the end of a project as just a deadline passed.
example: Sakurai's team has given him a wide variety of birthday presents, which he calls proof of a good relationship. The Game Arts core team for Brawl had played so much Melee that their analog stick ridges were worn down.
review_question: When did the team last do something together that wasn't work?
keywords: team morale culture celebration gratitude thanks icebreaker fun events motivation snacks recognition team building

principle: Line up the next plan before the team disbands
why: Teams scatter when a project ends, and directors usually go straight from one job to the next. Sakurai finished Smash Ultimate's 200-plus-page proposal on the same day as Smash for 3DS/Wii U's final video presentation, because staying ahead was the only way to keep the dev team together.
how_to_apply: During the tail end of a project, draft the follow-up proposal, including feature lists and per-character adjustments. Use any gap before a new team assembles to write design documents and win over key stakeholders.
anti_pattern: Starting the next plan from nothing after the team has already moved on.
example: Before Brawl's team assembled, Sakurai wrote the design documents and pitched each character to its original creator.
review_question: If this project ended next month, is a plan ready that would keep the team together?
keywords: next project pipeline continuity team retention proposal planning roadmap sequel
